modules.title: Coral Reef Ecosystems
modules.summary: Why coral reefs are the most biodiverse ecosystems in the ocean and what threatens them.

lessons.title: Rainforests of the sea
lessons.body: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor yet support roughly 25% of all marine species. They are built by tiny animals — coral polyps — that secrete calcium carbonate skeletons and live in partnership with photosynthetic algae called zooxanthellae. That partnership is why reefs thrive in clear, sunlit, nutrient-poor tropical water.

lessons.title: Why reefs matter to people
lessons.body: More than half a billion people depend on reefs for food, income, and coastal protection. Healthy reefs absorb wave energy and reduce erosion, shelter juvenile fish that stock coastal fisheries, and drive tourism economies. Losing a reef is not just an ecological loss — it is a social and economic one.

lessons.title: The threats
lessons.body: Rising sea temperatures cause bleaching, where stressed corals expel their algae and turn white; marine heatwaves can kill reefs in weeks. Ocean acidification slows skeleton growth, and local stressors — overfishing, sedimentation, and plastic debris — compound the damage. Coral reefs are the canary in the coal mine for ocean health.

quiz.question: What covers less than 1% of the ocean floor yet supports roughly 25% of all marine species?
What is the direct trigger of coral bleaching?
options: Sustained warm temperatures that stress corals

modules.title: Plastic Pollution in the Ocean
modules.summary: Where ocean plastic comes from, where it ends up, and why it persists for centuries.

lessons.title: The numbers
lessons.body: An estimated 8 to 12 million tonnes of plastic enter the ocean every year — roughly one garbage truck per minute (Jambeck et al., 2015). Most of it originates on land: uncollected waste, litter, and mismanaged landfill in coastal regions, carried to sea by rivers.

lessons.title: The garbage patches
lessons.body: Ocean currents concentrate floating debris into five major gyres, the largest being the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, which spans an area roughly three times the size of France. Despite the name, it is not a solid island — it is a diffuse soup of fragments, most of them below the surface and too small to see.

lessons.title: Why plastic persists
lessons.body: Plastic does not biodegrade; it photodegrades — sunlight breaks it into ever-smaller pieces called microplastics and nanoplastics. These particles are ingested by plankton, fish, seabirds, and marine mammals, entering food webs that include humans. Some plastic polymers take hundreds of years to break down, which is why prevention and collection both matter.

quiz.question: How much plastic is estimated to enter the ocean every year?
Why does plastic persist in the ocean for centuries?
options: It photodegrades into smaller fragments instead of breaking down
Marine bacteria cannot attach to it
It sinks below the reach of decomposers

modules.title: Underwater Robotics
modules.summary: How autonomous vehicles navigate, sense, and work beneath the surface.

lessons.title: ROVs and AUVs
lessons.body: Underwater robots come in two main flavors: remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), tethered to a surface ship and human-controlled, and autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), which follow pre-programmed missions without a cable. Modern systems blur the line, switching between supervised and autonomous modes based on the task.

lessons.title: Sensing the unseen
lessons.body: Radio waves do not travel through water, so robots navigate with acoustic sensors — sonar for mapping and obstacle avoidance, acoustic beacons for positioning. Optical cameras work only in clear, lit water, which is why many platforms pair them with sonar and environmental sensors like turbidity, conductivity, and dissolved-oxygen probes.

lessons.title: Collecting without destroying
lessons.body: Collecting debris on the seabed is an exercise in precision: currents push everything, visibility is short, and fragile habitats sit next to the waste. Robots use computer vision to identify targets, then approach slowly with suction or gripper tools designed to disturb as little sediment as possible. Gentle, targeted removal beats aggressive sweeping every time.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between an ROV and an AUV?
options: ROVs are tethered and human-controlled; AUVs run autonomous missions
AUVs are always larger than ROVs

quiz.question: Why do underwater robots rely on acoustic sensors for navigation?
options: Radio waves do not travel well through water
Sound waves travel slower in air

modules.title: Water Quality Monitoring
modules.summary: The core measurements that tell us whether water is healthy — and what changes reveal.

lessons.title: The essential measurements
lessons.body: The classic water quality suite covers temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, salinity, and turbidity. Temperature drives every biological rate; dissolved oxygen directly limits fish and invertebrate life; turbidity measures suspended particles that can smother habitats and block light. Sudden shifts in any of these are early warning signs.

lessons.title: Nutrients and pollution
lessons.body: Nitrates and phosphates from agricultural runoff and sewage feed algal blooms that can collapse oxygen levels — a process called eutrophication. Heavy metals, hydrocarbons, and microplastics persist in sediments and accumulate up the food chain. Monitoring programs track these compounds because they reveal human impact long before visible damage appears.

lessons.title: From sensors to decisions
lessons.body: A single reading is a snapshot; trends are the story. Continuous or repeated sampling lets scientists separate natural variation — tides, seasons, storms — from genuine decline. That is why modern monitoring combines fixed buoys, robotic surveys, and citizen-collected samples into one time series that managers can act on.

quiz.question: Which of these is part of the classic water quality measurement suite?
What does eutrophication cause in coastal waters?
options: Algal blooms that collapse oxygen levels

modules.title: Ocean Data & Citizen Science
modules.summary: How open data and public participation are changing the way we understand the ocean.

lessons.title: The open ocean data revolution
lessons.body: Satellites, Argo floats, and research ships produce petabytes of ocean data, but much of it was historically locked in institutional archives. Open initiatives like Copernicus Marine and EMODnet now publish near-real-time temperature, current, and chlorophyll data that anyone can use — the raw material behind ocean dashboards like this one.

lessons.title: Citizen science at scale
lessons.body: Volunteers can collect data that would otherwise be impossibly expensive: beach litter counts, reef observations, and water clarity readings. Programs like the NOAA Marine Debris Monitoring and the global iNaturalist community have logged millions of records. The catch is quality — consistent protocols and simple apps turn enthusiastic observers into reliable sensors.

lessons.title: Making data tell a story
lessons.body: Raw sensor readings do not move people; trends and maps do. Visualizing collection events as time series and locating them on a map turns a spreadsheet into an argument for action. Good ocean data projects design their data pipeline and their public interface together, so the evidence and the story stay connected.

quiz.question: Why do monitoring programs combine buoys, robotic surveys, and citizen samples?
options: It is cheaper than any single method
Repeated sampling separates real trends from natural variation
Buoys are the only instruments that collect plastic

quiz.question: What makes citizen science useful at ocean scale?
options: Consistent protocols turn many observers into reliable sensors
No training or tools are needed
It only works for fish counts

modules.title: Marine Restoration
modules.summary: What restoration really involves — from coral nurseries to mangrove replanting — and why prevention comes first.

lessons.title: Restoration is a craft, not a miracle
lessons.body: Restoring a marine habitat means rebuilding the conditions that let life return: clean water, stable substrate, and enough protection for young organisms to survive. Coral nurseries grow fragments on underwater frames before outplanting them onto degraded reefs; mangrove and seagrass projects replant pioneer species to stabilize sediment. Every project is measured in years, not weeks.

lessons.title: What makes projects succeed
lessons.body: The most successful restoration programs pair ecological work with community governance — local people who monitor, protect, and benefit from the restored habitat. They also choose the right sites: a polluted bay will kill replanted corals no matter how skilled the nursery. Site selection and threat removal come before any planting.

lessons.title: Prevention beats restoration
lessons.body: Restoration is slow, expensive, and uncertain; preventing damage is fast, cheap, and reliable. The math is stark: stopping plastic from entering the ocean and protecting existing reefs is orders of magnitude more effective than cleaning up afterwards. That is why every restoration plan in this program starts with a prevention mission.

quiz.question: What do coral nurseries do before outplanting fragments onto degraded reefs?
options: Remove all fish from the area

quiz.question: Why does prevention beat restoration in marine conservation?
options: Restoration is slow, expensive, and uncertain
Prevention is more visible to the public
